newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing steps up security ahead of HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Beijing steps up security ahead of HK handover.

text.p: Beijing police have been placed on alert against separatists, dissidents, beggars and the mentally deranged to ensure no domestic unrest ruffles the smooth handover of Hong Kong to China in July, Chinese sources said on Monday.

China has hailed the return of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty after 156 years of British colonial rule as one of the highlights of the year, if not the decade, and officials are determined to let nothing go wrong.
China's Communist Party chief and President Jiang Zemin plans to fly down to the territory for the handover ceremony at midnight on June 30, said one source, a senior government official.
Jiang would return to the Chinese capital after the ceremony ends and would not spend the night in Hong Kong, said the source, who asked not to be identified.
Hong Kong's Chinese-language Ming Pao newspaper said last week Premier Li Peng would attend other celebrations in the enclave.

In Beijing, police have been on high alert since a bomb exploded on a bus in a central shopping district on March 7. China's state-controlled media said no one died but several people were wounded in the attack.
Police have offered a reward, but have made no arrests.
Beijing was rocked by at least one other bombing in March, but no casualties were reported.
The bomb attacks have stunned China's leadership, which has been trying to put on a show of solidarity and stability after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19.

Police are jittery about China's tiny band of dissidents in the run-up to the eighth anniversary of demonstrations for democracy in Beijing's Tiananmen Square that were crushed by the Chinese army on June 4, 1989 with heavy loss of life.

Beijing police have orders to remove the mentally deranged, the jobless, the homeless and beggars from within a one-km (0.6-mile) radius of Tiananmen Square and the Workers' Stadium in the run-up to the handover, one source, a cabinet official, told Reuters. Handover celebrations are set for both sites.
"(The authorities) are worried about turmoil," said the source, who asked not to be identified.
Plainclothes police in key Beijing streets would be reinforced, the source said. Police holidays would be cancelled.
"On the outside it will look normal. But there will be a lot more plainclothes," the source said.
Chinese embassies overseas have been told to be more prudent when issuing visas to individuals, the source said.

Non-Beijing residents would be sent back to their hometowns if they were caught working in the capital without permits, he said. Hotels have been asked not to allow people without identification cards to check in.
Sports officials also have orders to cool off the soccer craze to avoid any football-linked unrest, another source said.
China's soccer mania runs at fever pitch and the incidence of unrest and minor disturbances involving fans disappointed or jubilant at the performance of their teams has increased in recent years.
